summary: The last 4 weeks have been severely disrupted by illness starting around 2 August, with doctor-ordered rest through at least 11 August — body battery readings have been critically low (0–11) across multiple recent days, confirming the athlete is still not recovered. Prior to the illness, training was sparse but included a solid 77km cycling effort on 20 July and reasonable swim volume; however, the high HR run on 18 July (avg 179 bpm) suggests that session was executed at too high an intensity relative to recovery. The immediate priority is a careful, gated return to training from 11 August, protecting the Half Oceanman (56 days away, 5km swim) and Treviso 10K (64 days away) rather than chasing lost fitness.
suggestions: On 11 August, treat the return-to-training run as a pure wellness check: keep HR strictly under 135 bpm and shorten to 20–25 minutes if any fatigue or symptoms persist — do not attempt both the run and the swim on the same day if body battery is below 40 on waking.

Given the Half Oceanman swim target of 5,000m at 2:30/100m in 56 days, prioritise swimming volume over cycling and running in weeks 9–10: aim for at least 3 swim sessions per week totalling 6,000–7,000m once fully recovered, as your open-water pace data shows you averaging around 2:25–2:35/100m which is right on the edge of target.

Avoid any runs at or above tempo intensity (sub-5:30/km) until at least one full week of easy running has been completed post-illness — the 18 July run at 179 bpm average shows a pattern of going too hard too soon, which likely contributed to reduced resilience heading into the illness period.

For the week abroad (24–30 August), confirm bike access in advance; if no bike is available, substitute the Saturday long ride with a 75–90 min open-water or pool swim, which directly serves the Half Oceanman build and requires no equipment.

Sleep is the single biggest lever right now — multiple nights of under 5 hours in the last two weeks will slow immune recovery and block training adaptation; target 7+ hours per night as a non-negotiable gate before resuming any quality sessions.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk8 easy return jog 30–35 min at HR ≤135 bpm or walk only
proposed_changes.proposed_session: 20–25 min easy walk/jog only if body battery on waking is ≥35; if body battery is below 35, replace with a 20-min gentle walk and postpone the jog to 12 August — do not combine with the swim on the same day.
proposed_changes.reason: Body battery has been at 0–11 for several consecutive days (Aug 3–6, Aug 8) and the athlete is only just reaching the end of the doctor-ordered rest window; splitting or shortening the first session reduces relapse risk.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk8 easy 30-min pool swim, 1,000–1,200m, technique drills only
proposed_changes.proposed_session: Move to 12 August (Wednesday, nominally a rest day) and keep at 1,000m max — only if the Tuesday run/walk felt fully comfortable and body battery has recovered above 40; skip entirely if still symptomatic.
proposed_changes.reason: Stacking a swim on top of the first run-back session on the same day is excessive given critically depleted body battery readings through 8 August; separating them by 24 hours reduces total daily stress on an immune system still recovering from illness.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk8 easy 45-min Z2 spin at 120–150W as a systems-check ride
proposed_changes.proposed_session: Reduce to 30 min at 100–130W (perceived easy, cadence 85–90 rpm) and skip if morning body battery is below 40 — this is still a systems-check only, not a fitness session.
proposed_changes.reason: The athlete will only be 2 days into return-to-training and wellness data shows a persistent pattern of very low body battery; keeping the ride shorter and below the original adjusted target limits cumulative stress in the first week back.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk9 Pool Swim Tuesday — min 2,000m, technique and aerobic sets at ≤2:30/100m
proposed_changes.proposed_session: Extend to 2,200–2,400m and include a 400m continuous time-trial effort at target 2:30/100m pace in the middle of the session (e.g. 400m warm-up, 4×400m with 30s rest, 200m cool-down) — this is the first Half Oceanman-specific swim stimulus.
proposed_changes.reason: With the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim 56 days away and the target pace at 2:30/100m, week 9 (if recovery gates are passed) is the right moment to introduce the first race-pace swim block and begin progressive distance build.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk9 Long Ride AI adjusted — morning OW swim 45–60 min then afternoon ride 75–80km at 128–177W
proposed_changes.proposed_session: Keep the morning open-water swim (1,500–2,000m at easy effort) as the primary session; reduce the afternoon ride to 60–70 min / 25–30km at 120–150W rather than 75–80km — cap total daily training load and cut the ride short if HR exceeds 145 bpm.
proposed_changes.reason: This is only the second weekend back from illness and stacking a full OW swim plus a 75–80km ride risks an excessive single-day load spike that could trigger relapse or excessive fatigue heading into the Treviso 10K build weeks.

proposed_changes.current_session: Wk10 Long Ride — 100km at 128–177W; if no bike available abroad, replace with 75-min swim
proposed_changes.proposed_session: If travelling abroad with no bike access, replace entirely with a 75–90 min open-water or pool swim (2,200–2,500m at 2:25–2:30/100m race pace) — this directly builds the Half Oceanman swim leg and requires no equipment; do not attempt to find a rental bike unless logistics are already confirmed.
proposed_changes.reason: Athlete is confirmed abroad the week of 24 August; bike access is uncertain, and with the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim being the nearest race target, a swim replacement session delivers more specific race value than a logistically uncertain ride.
